parsed.attack: Centriq is this product, already built and already dead: photograph an appliance nameplate, get the model identified, the manual, the parts that fit it, and a dated room-by-room record you could hand to a contractor or a buyer. It shut down on 31 January 2026 and took its users' home data with it - eight months ago, well after free on-device vision existed, which means the named unlock was already in the world and did not save it. Centriq also had what this idea does not: a curated parts database behind the recognition, so "which parts fit it" was an answered question rather than a model's guess. What killed it is the interval - a home equipment record is written in one afternoon and needed again two years later, and no consumer subscription survives a two-year gap between sessions, which is why the survivors in this category sell to agents, insurers and property managers instead.
parsed.strongest_defence: A single-unit landlord is not a homeowner: gas safety certificates, EICR cycles, tenant turnover and a plumber who has to be briefed give the record scheduled reasons to be opened that Centriq's homeowner never had.
parsed.verdict_reason: Centriq ran the identical wedge with a better parts database and shut down in January 2026, after the on-device unlock existed, on a cause - the years-long gap between capture and need, under a subscription - that this idea reproduces exactly.
